title: Introduction to Sets
summary: This Unit has provided a foundational overview of Set Theory, beginning with methods for representing collections through roster and set-builder notation, then moving to the structural hierarchy of subsets, power sets, and cardinality. Subsequently, visual logic and abstract operations, using Venn Diagrams to demonstrate set interactions such as unions and intersections, are discussed Also advanced logical concepts such as Russell’s Paradox and the geometry

Essential Terminology & Concepts

A Set A Core Definition

A Set A said to be a proper subset of a set B if A is a subset of B and A and B are not equal.

S Of A Space Core Definition

S Of A Space convex if and only if for any pair of points p and q in the set S, the line section from p to q is enclosed completely in the set of S, as done in the figure on L.

Sets Key Concept

Conventionally, the concept of number and geometric concepts like 'straight line', triangle' and 'square'.

Concept Of Set Key Concept

Set is a basic concept like 'point', & 'straight line' in geometry and like 'number' in arithmetic, and hence, should be left undefined.

Relationships Between Sets Key Concept

For any two sets X and Y, the set relationships that we discuss are: (i) equality (=) of X and Y (ii) X is a subset/ superset (⸦) of Y (iii) X is a proper subset/superset(⸦)of Y, and (iv) is not a subset of ( ).

1.2.1 Concept of Set

  • Set is a basic concept like 'point', & 'straight line' in geometry and like 'number' in arithmetic, and hence, should be left undefined.
  • Roughly, a set may be considered a collection of things or entities, such as names of animals, names of books, names of numbers, names of geometrical shapes, or any mixture of these.
  • Any entity in a set is called a member, or an element, of that set.
  • Further, in a set, no member is written more than once.

1.2.3 Methods of Representing a Set

  • For any two sets X and Y, the set relationships that we discuss are: (i) equality (=) of X and Y (ii) X is a subset/ superset (⸦) of Y (iii) X is a proper subset/superset(⸦)of Y, and (iv) is not a subset of ( ).

  • ii) X is said to be a subset of Y if every element of X is an element of Y.

1.2.4 Cardinality of a Set

  • The number of elements in a finite set say A is called its Cardinality or cardinal number of a finite set and is denoted by n(A).
  • For example, (i) If A = {x, y, z}, then n(A) = 3, i.e.
  • (ii) If B = {1,4, 2, 3, 9, 15}, then n(B) = 6, i.e.

1.2.5 Subsets

  • Before we relook at the subset, let us define the empty set.
  • The empty set (also known as the null set) is a unique concept in mathematics and set theory.
  • It represents a set that contains no elements.
  • It is denoted by or { } : A pair of curly braces with nothing between them.

1.2.6 Power Set of a Set

  • Definitions: The power set of a set A is the set of all the subsets of A, and is denoted by P(A).
  • Sometimes power set of a given set A is denoted by 2A, because that is the Cardinality of the power set A.
  • For example, the set {1, 2, 3} has 3 elements, and, the power set of A, viz.

1.3 Types of Sets

  • We have seen that set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects.
  • Also repetition of elements in a set is not allowed.
  • So once a set is defined, automatically number of elements contained by it has also become fixed.
  • In this section, we shall discuss the different names given to a set on the bases of the number of elements contained by the set.
